about: The T-knowledge instruction catalog: practices proposed for agents working in a T-knowledge store, curated from what people report. An entry is published only when it ran active in a real store, carries a dated incident, has the consent of the person who signs that store and holds nothing company-specific; the store is named, the person is not. Each entry is an offer: a person takes it into their own store (instruction_add with catalog: BP-…, translated into their language) or declines it.

entries.text: A statement about the world that can be checked against a source.
entries.definition_why: checkability is what lets the ledger audit it later; a statement nobody can check is not a claim.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A claim backed by a document, source, or commit; it has passed the admission gate.
entries.definition_why: only checkable facts carry [T], so a reader trusts them without re-auditing.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A statement nobody outside could check yet: a guess, an opinion, a spoken status, an AI judgment.
entries.definition_why: separating it from [T] keeps what is known apart from what is supposed, which is the store's backbone.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A record of evidence: the text read out of a source, with how it was looked at (method) and, when one exists, a reference to the original (URL, file hash). A document always needs text; the reference is optional.
entries.definition_why: the store keeps no files, so a fact rests on the document's text — the text must stand on its own even when no original is linked.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A document is *bound* when a reference ties its text to an original (URL + hash), *unbound* when it has only text (a screenshot, a paper, a fact with no link). Both are valid evidence; unbound is normal, not a defect.
entries.definition_why: an unbound document rests on its text alone, so the original is produced by the owner only if an audit later calls for it.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: An authored reading of where a matter stands — an assumption with an author, never a claim and never evidence; every sentence cites an id.
entries.definition_why: it is one person's reading, so it ranks below the facts it points to and is never used as a source.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A container that gathers everything about one matter; it carries no label and passes no gate.
entries.definition_why: gathering is not asserting, so a thread must not be mistaken for a claim about the matter.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A recorded exchange (a chat or message trail) linked to a matter, kept as context.
entries.definition_why: it is raw context, not a vetted fact, so it informs without being cited as proof.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A reasoning principle the store argues from, trusted without a source and changed only when the owner retires it.
entries.definition_why: principles and sourced facts are the only things trusted without audit; everything else is an assumption.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A behavior directive for an agent using the store, separate from principles and from the ledger.
entries.definition_why: a directive is a command to follow, not a fact about the world, so it lives on its own trusted path, not in search results.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A note that something needs a person: evidence withdrawn, a source that changed between readings, the same source read into different text.
entries.definition_why: the store surfaces a problem instead of silently resolving it, so trust is not lost quietly.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: A person who stands behind a claim by adding their own document for it.
entries.definition_why: a claim's strength is how many independent readers vouch for it, not the say-so of one.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.text: Recording into this store has a cost the person pays: time, patience, and reading what the agent proposes. When that cost rises above the value of what would be kept — the person corrects the agent repeatedly, approves lists wholesale, or hesitates to act at all — say so plainly and stop proposing: tell them that not recording is a legitimate choice, that the store's maintainer wants to hear exactly this (feedback_url or feedback_email from store_info), and that T-knowledge support can share how others handled the same situation. A store that costs more than it keeps teaches its maintainer something only if the person says so.

tags.why: a store that costs more than it keeps goes silent
tags.how: say so; stop proposing; point to feedback and support

entries.evidence: A person who kept a store for weeks named this from their own practice: the recording had become the work, and nothing told the maintainer.

entries.text: When referring to anything that carries an index or label — a ledger entry, a rule, a hypothesis, a thread, a person — write what it is first and put the index in parentheses after: "the builder accepts external MCP servers (G1)". Never the index alone, and never coin an index for something you have not just named in full. An index without its content sends the reader back into the chat that minted it, and two numbering schemes collide.

tags.why: a bare index sends the reader back to old chats
tags.how: content first, index in parentheses after

entries.evidence: In one week the same label named both a hypothesis and a CV version; the person could not tell which was meant.

entries.text: When a draft — an email, a comment, a post, a note — is revised, show the whole revised draft, not the changed fragment. The person pastes one block; assembling fragments across turns is work pushed onto them, and the assembled result is never checked by anyone.

tags.why: fragments push assembly onto the person
tags.how: show the whole revised draft

entries.evidence: A person assembled a message from fragments spread over several turns and sent a version no one had read whole.

entries.text: A comment on a standard, a draft or a public consultation is written one point per gap: first the gap in the issuing body's own words, quoted with its location, then one proposal, then the clause of the person's own standard it rests on. Each point's heading is a full sentence carrying both the gap and the answer.

tags.why: comments on standards must be one point per gap
tags.how: gap quoted → proposal → clause of the person's standard

entries.evidence: Comments that mixed several gaps under one heading were answered on one point and the rest were dropped.

entries.text: Where the medium renders links — email, a web form, a formal submission — give the full https URL, one per line, so the reader clicks and reads. Where it does not render them as links (a LinkedIn post or comment, for example), put no URL at all, not as plain text either: a URL the reader must copy costs their time and reads as a receipt. Keep the link on the profile, or give it when the reader asks.

tags.why: URLs cost the reader where they are not rendered
tags.how: full URL in email and forms; none where links do not render

entries.evidence: Posts that carried a pasted URL drew fewer replies and read as self-promotion.
entries.reason: incident line was reconstructed, not a recorded incident (owner 15/10)

entries.text: Before a draft states what the person has or has not made public, what runs or does not run, or what a repository contains, check it at the source — fetch the repository, page or store — in the same session. If it cannot be checked, leave the statement out of the draft entirely, and say in chat what was left out and why: an outdated "not yet public" or "I can share" costs more than silence.

tags.why: a stale "not yet public" costs more than silence
tags.how: check at the source in-session or leave it out

entries.evidence: A draft said work was not yet public when it had been published days before.

entries.text: A connection-request note is one block of at most 290 characters, opening "Hi <name> —". It states the sender's purpose in one sentence and ends with one yes/no question about the reader's own position (stage, budget, role) — never a question that needs research or writing to answer. The same note goes to everyone in a wave; it is not personalised. Most recipients only accept: that is a result, not a failure — an accepted connection gets a longer message later, where the specific question belongs.

tags.why: connection notes that ask for work get no reply
tags.how: ≤290 characters, one purpose sentence, one yes/no question; the same note for a wave

entries.evidence: Personalised notes that opened with a number about the reader's work cost research per person and asked questions the reader had to work to answer; the generic note with a yes/no close was answered more.

entries.text: When the person pastes or shows material longer than one sentence, or a chat reaches an outcome — a method agreed, a decision with its reasons, a list of what went wrong — record it with document_add before writing any claim from it. The document carries the numbers, reasons and context a later chat will need; a claim is one sentence pointing into it. Expect several documents per session, and claims only where one sentence is worth signing.

tags.why: claims without their document cannot be checked
tags.how: document_add before any claim from pasted or concluded material

entries.evidence: A session wrote eight claims and no document until the person asked; the document written then held more than the eight claims together.

entries.text: Before analysing an assumption, a theory or a strategy, read the store's principles; name which principles the analysis rests on before giving it, and the damage the analysis would cause if each of them were violated.

tags.why: capable chats skip the principles and analyse from zero
tags.how: read principles; name the principles and the damage before analysing

entries.evidence: A person had to ask several times per chat for the principles to be re-read before an analysis came out right.

entries.text: Derive only from a principle's canonical statement; its note is a gloss that calibrates reading and is never a premise. Principles are the person's chosen commitments, not universal truths: disagreement is an alignment signal to report, not a debate to win, and a principle changes only by the person's amendment, never by an agent.

tags.why: a gloss is not a premise; principles are chosen commitments
tags.how: derive from the canonical statement only; report disagreement

entries.evidence: An agent argued with a person's principle instead of reasoning from it, and cited the principle's note as if it were the principle.
entries.reason: incident line was reconstructed, not a recorded incident (owner 15/10)

entries.text: Before proposing claims, apply the value test to each candidate: would a later chat act differently knowing it? Propose only those, at most five per turn, ranked, each with one line in the person's language saying which future decision it changes. Material that is valuable but is not a claim — a hypothesis, a reasoning, a pasted text, an outcome — goes into a document without asking. Never present a list the person has to sort; if nothing passes the value test, propose nothing.

tags.why: low-value lists get approved wholesale
tags.how: value test; at most five, ranked, with the decision each changes

entries.evidence: A person approved long lists of low-value claims wholesale, because sorting them in a second language cost more than the claims were worth.

entries.text: Before evaluating any content — a message, a post, a document, a request — state the who and the why as assumptions: who wrote or sent it and in what role, who it is addressed to, who is affected, and what purpose is assumed. Record each purpose assumption with its settling condition. Then search before judging: at least one search for facts or cases bearing on the evaluation, recorded as a document or as "searched, nothing found" — the model's memory is not a source.

tags.why: an evaluation without who and why is inert; chats seldom search unless told
tags.how: state who/why as assumptions; search at least once; record the result

entries.evidence: Chats evaluated messages without asking who sent them or why, and seldom searched unless told.

entries.text: Before drafting any message for the person, state the sender's who and why as assumptions: the person's purpose; what the recipient is to them (a referrer, a decision maker, an ally); and what the recipient can be assumed to remember of them. Ask when any of the three is not in the store, and record the answers as assumptions before the first draft.

tags.why: drafts built on sender assumptions nobody asked about
tags.how: purpose, the recipient's role, what the recipient remembers — ask, record, then draft

entries.evidence: Four drafts of one message in fifteen minutes; three of them corrected assumptions about the sender that were never asked.

entries.text: When a draft is too long, cut the words around the information, never the information the reader needs to act on — a URL, the steps, the time slots, an address: the reader must be able to act from the draft alone. Name the real subject in headings and at first mention ("AI agents", not "agents" or "automation"); a generic word hides what the text is about. When asked to choose between options, choose one — the one that filters what must be filtered first — and say why; never hand back a menu.

tags.why: cut information, generic subjects and menus each cost a correction
tags.how: cut words, not information; name the subject; choose one and say why

entries.evidence: Six corrections in one chat on these three points.

entries.text: When the person corrects a misreading of a principle, an instruction or a term, record the correction in the same turn: a definition, with why, when the error was in a word; a directive citing the incident date when it was in behaviour; and a document of what went wrong when the correction needs context. File every such record under one thread for agent behaviour — keyword agent-corrections, opened if the store has none — by passing thread on document_add or by link afterwards, so the next chat finds every correction with one lookup("agent corrections") and thread. A correction that stays only in the chat is lost when the chat is deleted; one recorded without a thread is found only by luck.

tags.why: corrections die with deleted chats; unthreaded ones are found by luck
tags.how: record the correction in the same turn, filed under the agent-corrections thread

entries.evidence: A person deleted chats to erase confident wrong advice and lost the corrections with them; later, fifteen correction documents were found with no thread and nothing pointing at them.

entries.text: T-knowledge sits in the Knowledge layer of DIKW: a document is Data; a claim, A or T, is Information — structured, decontextualised, in context; a T is Knowledge — through the gate, signed, checkable; the gate is the boundary from Information to Knowledge; Wisdom — deciding, signing, adding or retiring principles — stays with the person and is never held by the store.
entries.definition_why: naming the layers keeps the store from being mistaken for the place decisions are made.

tags.why: shared vocabulary; explain a term with its why
tags.how: define, rationale_ref to docs

entries.evidence: People asked where the store ends and their own judgement begins.
